lead: A particle is a body whose size we ignore, so every force on it passes through one point (see Chapter 1.1). Equilibrium means those forces add to zero; one vector equation decides the problem. The same calculation holds a hanging lamp, a knot in a crane rope and a cable between two poles. In a plane it gives two scalar equations. With exactly three forces it becomes Lami's theorem.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.4 for vector sums of concurrent forces and Chapter 1.5 for free body diagrams.

blocks.text: A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of forces on it is zero. Newton's second law then gives zero acceleration: the particle is at rest or moves in a straight line at constant speed. Statics uses the at-rest case — a knot, hook or joint that does not move.

blocks.where: ΣF is the vector sum of every external force. Zero means the forces cancel in direction and size, not that each is zero.

blocks.text: Resolve each force into components (see Chapter 1.3). Choose x and y axes. A force of magnitude F at angle θ from the positive x axis has components F cos θ along x and F sin θ along y. The vector equation splits into two scalar equations.

blocks.where: Fx and Fy are components in newtons (N); θ is measured anticlockwise from positive x. Both equations must hold together.

blocks.text: Two equations fix at most two unknowns — usually two tension magnitudes, or one tension and one angle. Three unknown magnitudes cannot be found from statics alone.

items: Draw the free body diagram of the particle only.
Count the forces. More than three usually means use components.
Choose axes; align one axis with an unknown force if that removes an angle.
Write ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, keep signs by direction, and solve.
Substitute both answers into the other equation as a check.

blocks.text: Suppose exactly three coplanar forces meet at one point and keep a particle in equilibrium. Then each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two forces gives the same number.
P / sin α = Q / sin β = R / sin γ
blocks.where: P, Q, R are magnitudes in N; α is the angle between Q and R (facing P); β is between P and R; γ is between P and Q. The three angles sum to 360°.

blocks.text: Proof. Draw the three forces tip to tail. Their sum is zero, so they close into a triangle with sides P, Q, R. Inside that triangle, the angle between sides Q and R is 180° − α, because Q and R keep their directions. The sine rule gives P / sin A = Q / sin B = R / sin C, and sin(180° − α) = sin α. Replacing each triangle angle gives Lami's theorem.
The naming trips people up. α is the angle made by the other two force lines, opening towards P — not the angle beside P. In the lamp below, T₁ pairs with 150°, not its own 30° tilt.

items: Exactly three forces, all meeting at one point, all in one plane. Four or more forces break the triangle argument.
Every force must appear once on the left side; the weight counts as a force.
Use Lami for a quick check even when you solved by components.

blocks.text: Lami's theorem is a shortcut, not a separate law, so it cannot give an answer that components would miss. Use it when three angles are given and the forces lie awkwardly between the axes. Use components when forces are along x and y, when there are four or more forces, or when one force direction is unknown.

A crane hook often carries three forces: two sling tensions and the load. If sling angles are given, Lami gives both tensions quickly. With a tag line attached there are four forces, and only component equations are safe.
Measure each angle between the two force lines themselves. Check that the three angles add to 360°. If one angle comes out negative, you measured between the wrong pair of forces.

figure.caption: Knot O held by two strings with a 100 N lamp below. T₁ pairs with the 150° angle between T₂ and the weight; T₂ pairs with the 120° angle between T₁ and the weight.

spec.aria: Three forces meet at knot O: a 50 N string up to the left at 150°, an 86.6 N string up to the right at 60°, and a 100 N weight hanging straight down.

examples.question: A lamp of weight 100 N hangs from a knot O. String OA runs 30° above the horizontal towards the left; string OB runs 60° above the horizontal towards the right. The knot is at rest. Find the tensions T₁ in OA and T₂ in OB, using Lami's theorem, and verify by components.
steps: Free body diagram of O: three forces only — T₁ along OA at 150° from positive x, T₂ along OB at 60°, W = 100 N straight down at 270°.
Angle between the strings = 180° − 30° − 60° = 90°. This is γ, the angle facing W.
Angle facing T₁ is between T₂ and W: 90° + 60° = 150°. Call it α.
Angle facing T₂ is between T₁ and W: 90° + 30° = 120°. Call it β. Check: 90° + 150° + 120° = 360°.
Lami: T₁ / sin 150° = T₂ / sin 120° = 100 / sin 90°.
The common value is 100 / 1 = 100 N. So T₁ = 100 × sin 150° = 100 × 0.5 = 50 N.
y check: 86.6 sin 60° + 50 sin 30° − 100 = 75 + 25 − 100 = 0. Both equations hold.
examples.answer: T₁ = 50 N and T₂ = 86.6 N, both tensions pulling away from the knot.
examples.check:
import math
W = 100.0
den = math.sin(math.radians(90))
T1 = W * math.sin(math.radians(150)) / den
T2 = W * math.sin(math.radians(120)) / den
print(round(T1, 1))
print(round(T2, 1))

traps: Dividing a force by the sine of an angle next to it instead of the angle between the other two forces. T₁ goes with 150°, never with its own 30°.
Using Lami's theorem on four or more forces, or on forces that do not all pass through one point. The closed triangle proof fails.
Leaving the weight out of the free body diagram, then wondering why the two tensions do not balance each other.
Measuring every angle from a different reference line and mixing signs in ΣFx and ΣFy. Fix one axis and measure all angles from it.
Calculator set to radians while the question is in degrees, or typing sin 120 as a negative number without thinking.

quiz.q: State Lami's theorem and define each angle in it.
quiz.a: If three coplanar concurrent forces P, Q, R keep a particle in equilibrium, then P / sin α = Q / sin β = R / sin γ, where α is the angle between Q and R, β between P and R, and γ between P and Q.

quiz.q: Why does Lami's theorem stop working when a fourth force is added at the knot?
quiz.a: The proof closes three forces into a triangle and uses the sine rule. Four forces close into a quadrilateral, which has no single sine-rule relation. Equilibrium ΣF = 0 still holds, so use ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.

quiz.q: In the lamp problem, why is the angle facing T₁ equal to 150° and not 30°?
quiz.a: Lami pairs each force with the angle between the other two. Facing T₁ are T₂ and W; their angle is 90° + 60° = 150°. The 30° is beside T₁ and is not used.

quiz.q: A 100 N weight hangs from a knot on two strings that are equally inclined, each making 45° with the horizontal. Find each tension.
quiz.a: Angle between strings = 90°; angle facing each tension = 135°; angle facing weight = 90°. Lami: T / sin 135° = 100 / sin 90°, so T = 100 × 0.7071 = 70.7 N in each string.

quiz.q: A knot is pulled by 30 N towards the right and 40 N upwards. Find the single force that keeps it in equilibrium.
quiz.a: The required force is the equilibrant, opposite the resultant. Resultant magnitude = √(30² + 40²) = 50 N at 53.1° above positive x. So the third force is 50 N at 53.1° below negative x, down and to the left.

quiz.q: Three known forces act at a knot and the three angles between them are known. How can Lami's theorem be used without solving for anything?
quiz.a: Compute P / sin α, Q / sin β, R / sin γ. Equal values mean equilibrium is possible; unequal values mean it is not, so another force must be present.

quiz.q: A student resolves a force pointing down and to the left as +F cos θ and +F sin θ with θ measured from the positive x axis. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: For a force down-left, θ from positive x is between 180° and 270°, so cos θ and sin θ are already negative. Adding extra plus signs puts components in the wrong quadrant. Keep the signs produced by θ.

beyond: Not for the exam. In space the zero-sum idea gives three equations (see Chapter 1.7). For a whole structure every joint writes its own pair; this is the method of joints in Unit 3. Software assembles many node equations into one matrix. Cable and guy-wire design, transmission-tower rigging and scaffolding checks begin with a knot in equilibrium. Search next for 'method of joints', 'cable statics' and 'three-force body'.
